title: The Letter E on the Forehead
text:
In a set of experiments published in 2006, Adam Galinsky and his colleagues tested whether feeling powerful makes it harder to see the world from someone else's point of view.

First, they put participants in a powerful or a powerless frame of mind by asking them to write about a time they had power over someone, or a time someone had power over them. Then came a simple task: draw a capital letter E on your own forehead with a marker. There are two ways to do it. You can draw it so that it reads correctly to yourself, which means it looks backward to anyone facing you, or you can draw it so that it reads correctly to an observer.

People who had been primed to feel powerful were almost three times as likely to draw the E the self-oriented way. In other experiments in the same paper, powerful participants were also worse at judging what others knew and at reading emotions in faces. Galinsky and his team concluded that power tends to anchor people in their own perspective.
lesson: Power makes it easier to forget how things look from the other side. Before deciding, ask how your message will read to the people facing you.
people: Adam Galinsky, Joe Magee, M. Ena Inesi, Deborah Gruenfeld
source: Galinsky, A. D., Magee, J. C., Inesi, M. E., and Gruenfeld, D. H. (2006). Power and perspectives not taken. Psychological Science, 17(12), 1068-1074.
caveat: Later replication attempts of power priming effects have been mixed, so treat the size of the effect with caution.
